---
title: "Is Milan absorbing the North?"
subtitle: "Milan, the old industrial triangle and the core–periphery model, 2008–2023"
author: "Jacopo · Paper 7 Supervision 3"
toc: false
---

**The question.** Is northern Italy collapsing into a single core around Milan, as the core–periphery model predicts, or did the old industrial cities (Turin, Genoa) stall because of what they specialised in? Or did the decline of their industries trigger the move towards Milan?

## The answer

Northern Italy is not collapsing into a single core around Milan. Milan is the North's strongest labour market, and its lead in jobs has grown. But graduates and knowledge jobs, the mobile factors that the core–periphery model says should concentrate in the core, are no more concentrated in Milan today than they were in 2008 (knowledge jobs) or 2001 (graduates), and several other cities have grown alongside it. Turin's and Genoa's weaker performance is better explained by problems specific to each city than by Milan's pull.

## The three hypotheses

| | Hypothesis | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Milan's pull.** Graduates and firms concentrate in Milan (Forslid–Ottaviano version of Krugman's core–periphery model) | <span class="verdict">Fails in its strong form</span>: Milan grows, but it does not absorb the North |
| **B** | **Industry decline.** Turin and Genoa stalled because their industries declined | <span class="verdict">Holds only narrowly</span>: Turin's particular industry, not manufacturing as such |
| **C** | **Shock, then amplification.** The industry decline came first, then Milan's pull made it worse | <span class="verdict">Timing fits, mechanism doesn't</span>: Turin declines after 2014, but shows no graduate outflow |

The best overall account combines a narrow version of B for Turin with a separate, logistics-related decline for Genoa, while Milan grows alongside other cities rather than at their expense.
